newsitem.title: USA: Don't change world bank regulation much -- Greenspan.
newsitem.headline: Don't change world bank regulation much -- Greenspan.

text.p: Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan admitted on Tuesday that regulators might lack the expertise to oversee large global financial firms, but neverthless saw no need for a radical change in supervision.

In a speech prepared for delivery to the Institute of International Finance, the U.S. central bank chief argued that regulators should not try to prevent all bank failures, just stop them from becoming widespread.
"For the most part, these failures are a normal and important part of the market process and provide discipline," Greenspan said.

The Fed chief described the role of central banks as providing "catatrophic financial insurance coverage" in the financial system through their provision of discount window and other loans to private banks in distress.

"Such a subsidy should be reserved only for the rarest of disasters," Greenspan said. Otherwise, it would encourage recklessness among financial institutions that gambled on being bailed out by their central bank.
He questioned whether supervisors have the expertise and the resources to provide "meaningful" oversight of the risks taken by large, diversified, global financial institutions.
"The answer ... might well be (no)," Greenspan said.

Nevertheless, the Fed chief opposed any radical change in the current framework of international supervision, arguing that continued, steady improvement in oversight was the best strategy to try to ensure financial stability.

"While many firms should reassess and upgrade their risk management procedures and supervisors should improve their procedures, I do not believe that the need for a radical change in our framework for the supervision of internationally active financial firms has been demonstrated," he said.

Although the globalization of finance brought on by technological advance "clearly" calls for international cooperation among supervisors, Greenspan questioned whether formal arrangements for coordination were needed.

He said that supervisors and financial institutions have tried to use technolgy in recent years to better assess and manage risk. But he also acknowledged that technological advances were not without some risks.
"In some respects they have increased the potential for more rapid and widespread disruption," the Fed chief said.
